Those have a long way to go before I will trust them. Just this month there were multiple incidents in Denver where they drove through roads closed either for construction, or farmers markets. Though no one was hurt, there have been innumerable other instances where they have gotten people seriously injured and almost killed in some circumstances. They will drive into flooded intersections and stall, they've driven through active crime scenes, and many other things. The scarriest flaw in their technology is that they can easily be stopped by attackers that want to harm or rob you, all someone has to do is stand in front of the car, or climb on it, and the vehicle will not move, nor can operators override it, leaving the occupants at the mercy of the attackers. A human on the other hand could just quickly drive off. This has already occurred in a high profile incident in San Francisco in July. The person was lucky to escape, it took the police 35 minutes to respond. Luckily the assailant was just some dude dusted out of his mind, but imagine what he could have done with focused intent. Frankly I'm surprised that professional criminal rings haven't exploited this yet, but it's only a matter of time. And what about the risk of abduction?same scenario, a group of armed human trafficers surround the vehicle and take your kid out of it, and there is absolutely nothing Waymo can do to stop it. It's vehicles have absolutely no escape and evade programming, and are completely paralyzed when blocked by human obstacles. Some people will say that they are statically far safer, but I'm not so sure. Those statistics are heavily skewed and misnatched, because they only drive 207 million miles a year, whereas humans drive over 3 trillion. So you'll forgive me if I kindly disregard those statistics.
